title: Emily and Greg, Lakisha and Jamal
text:
Employers rarely admit to discrimination, and surveys about it are easy to answer dishonestly. In 2001 and 2002 the economists Marianne Bertrand of the University of Chicago and Sendhil Mullainathan of MIT tested it directly.

They answered more than 1,300 help-wanted ads in Boston and Chicago newspapers, in sales, administrative support, clerical and customer service jobs, sending nearly 5,000 fictitious resumes. For each ad they sent several resumes, some of higher and some of lower quality. Each resume was randomly given a name that sounded very typical for either white Americans, such as Emily Walsh or Greg Baker, or African Americans, such as Lakisha Washington or Jamal Jones. Otherwise the resumes were comparable. The researchers then counted how many received calls or e-mails inviting an interview.

Resumes with white-sounding names received about 50 percent more callbacks than otherwise comparable resumes with African American-sounding names. A white-sounding name was worth about as much as eight additional years of experience. Improving the quality of a resume raised callbacks substantially for white-sounding names but much less for African American-sounding ones. The gap appeared across occupations and industries, and even among employers who described themselves in their ads as equal opportunity employers.
lesson: Bias often works quietly in decisions that feel fair. Where you judge others, from hiring to grading, set up ways to judge the work before you see the name.
source: Bertrand, M., and Mullainathan, S. (2004). Are Emily and Greg more employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A field experiment on labor market discrimination. American Economic Review, 94(4), 991-1013.
